music-production-002.p: What does bit depth in digital audio primarily describe?
o: The precision of each amplitude measurement
How many measurements are taken per second
The tempo of the audio file
music-production-002.e: A greater bit depth gives more possible amplitude levels and therefore greater precision.

music-production-004.p: What bit depth does a standard audio CD use?
music-production-004.e: An audio CD uses 16-bit linear PCM.

music-production-013.p: Which pickup pattern is most sensitive at the front and least sensitive at the back of the microphone?
music-production-013.e: Cardioid is also called the kidney pattern and is often used to isolate a sound source.

music-production-014.p: What characterises a microphone with an omnidirectional pickup pattern?
o: It picks up sound from all directions
It picks up mostly sound from the front
It picks up from the front and back
music-production-014.e: An omnidirectional microphone has roughly the same sensitivity all the way round.

music-production-015.p: What is the proximity effect of a directional microphone?
o: More bass when the source is close
Less treble with a long cable
music-production-015.e: The proximity effect can give a close voice more body, but it can also make it muddy.

music-production-017.p: What does a pop filter mainly reduce during vocal recording?
o: Strong blasts of air from plosives
music-production-017.e: Consonants such as p and b can send a blast of air towards the capsule; the pop filter breaks up the airflow.

music-production-019.p: When does a compressor normally begin to reduce gain?
o: When the signal passes the threshold
music-production-019.e: The threshold sets the level at which compression begins to work.

music-production-020.p: What does a compressor ratio of 4:1 above the threshold mean?
o: 4 dB in gives about 1 dB out
1 dB in gives about 4 dB out
The signal is immediately lowered by 4 dB
The threshold is moved 4 dB per dB
music-production-020.e: The ratio describes the relationship between the level change above the threshold at the input and at the output.

music-production-021.p: What controls the attack of a compressor?
o: How wide the stereo signal is
How many frequency bands are processed
music-production-021.e: A longer attack can let the first transient pass before gain reduction reaches full strength.

music-production-022.p: What controls the release of a compressor?
o: How quickly the compression lets go again
How many overtones an oscillator has
How far the microphone is from the source
music-production-022.e: Release determines how gain returns to normal when the signal falls below the threshold.

music-production-029.p: What is a notch filter suited for?
o: Removing a very narrow frequency range
music-production-029.e: A narrow notch can target a resonance or a particular hum tone without changing much else.

music-production-032.p: What does predelay on a reverb control?
o: The time before the reverb tail starts
The time between two MIDI notes
music-production-032.e: Predelay creates a gap between the direct sound and the first clear reflections.

music-production-037.p: How many channels does MIDI 1.0 normally have per port?
music-production-037.e: MIDI 1.0 Channel Voice Messages contain a channel number from 1 to 16.

music-production-038.p: What does velocity describe in a standard MIDI Note On message?
o: The strength of the key strike as a numeric value
The length of the note in milliseconds
The tempo of the whole project
music-production-038.e: Velocity normally ranges from 0 to 127 and can control both volume and timbre, depending on the instrument.

music-production-039.p: What is MIDI CC 1 traditionally associated with?
music-production-039.e: Control Change 1 is defined as the modulation wheel or lever.

music-production-040.p: What is MIDI CC 7 traditionally associated with?
music-production-040.e: Control Change 7 is the volume parameter of the MIDI channel.

music-production-044.p: What does ADSR stand for in an envelope?
music-production-044.e: ADSR describes four stages in how a parameter evolves after a note is triggered and released.

music-production-048.p: What does polyphony mean for a synthesiser?
o: How many notes it can play at the same time
How many plug-ins can be installed
How many audio files can be exported
How many MIDI ports the computer has
music-production-048.e: A monophonic synth plays one note at a time; a polyphonic synth can play chords.

music-production-049.e: A DAW brings recording, editing, MIDI, mixing and often mastering together in one software environment.

music-production-050.p: What is a bus in a mix?
o: A shared signal path for several tracks
A filter that only removes bass
music-production-050.e: Several tracks can be sent to the same bus for shared level control or processing.

music-production-053.p: What can happen when two almost identical signals are out of phase?
o: They can cancel each other out
They are shifted in time but have equal volume
music-production-053.e: Opposing waveform movements add up poorly and can thin out certain frequencies in particular.

music-production-054.p: What is a send/return route particularly suited for?
o: Sharing the same effect between several tracks
music-production-054.e: Several tracks can send different amounts to, for example, the same reverb on a return channel.

music-production-058.e: BPM is a practical way of stating musical tempo.

music-production-064.p: What is the Step Sequencer in FL Studio especially suited for?
music-production-064.e: The Step Sequencer is a pattern-based grid that makes it quick to program drums, among other things.

music-production-066.p: What does one normally hear when FL Studio's transport is set to PAT?
music-production-066.e: Pattern Mode repeats the selected pattern, while Song Mode plays the arrangement in the Playlist.

music-production-067.p: What does FL Studio play in Song Mode?
o: The list in the Plugin Picker
music-production-067.e: Song Mode follows the clips and structure in the Playlist rather than only the currently selected pattern.

music-production-068.p: Which function key normally opens the Piano roll in FL Studio?
music-production-068.e: F7 shows the Piano roll; F5 shows the Playlist, F6 the Channel Rack and F9 the Mixer.

music-production-069.p: Which function key normally shows the Mixer in FL Studio?
music-production-069.e: F9 shows or hides the Mixer window.

music-production-070.p: Which function key normally shows the Playlist in FL Studio?
music-production-070.e: F5 shows or hides the Playlist window.

music-production-071.p: Which function key normally opens the Plugin Picker in FL Studio?
music-production-071.e: F8 opens the Plugin Picker, where instruments and effects can be chosen visually.

music-production-072.p: What does the F4 shortcut normally do in FL Studio?
o: Turns the metronome on or off
music-production-072.e: F4 selects the next free pattern and opens its naming.

music-production-073.p: What normally happens when you create an Automation Clip in FL Studio?
o: The control is copied to all patterns
The value is saved as a mixer preset
The control is linked to the master tempo
music-production-073.e: Automation Clips store curves that control knobs and parameters across the arrangement.

music-production-075.p: What do Ghost Notes mean in FL Studio's Piano roll?
o: Other channels' notes shown for reference
Deleted notes are shown until you save
Notes outside the scale are hidden
music-production-075.e: Ghost Notes make it easier to write harmonies by showing notes from other channels in the same pattern.

music-production-076.p: What does the Quantize tool do in FL Studio's Piano roll?
o: Aligns notes to a rhythmic grid
Adjusts the notes to one particular chord
Doubles the velocity of all notes
Turns MIDI data into an audio file
music-production-076.e: Quantize moves timing to a chosen grid or groove.

music-production-078.p: What does the Alt key normally do while dragging a note in FL Studio's Piano roll?
o: Locks the note to the root
music-production-078.e: Holding Alt while moving a note lets it be placed without the selected snap division.

music-production-082.p: Where does Edison primarily work with the loaded audio?
music-production-082.e: Edison works in RAM, so it suits samples and shorter recordings rather than many hours of audio.

music-production-083.p: What is the result of Edison's command with the arrow pointing at the arrangement?
o: The selection becomes a new Audio Clip
The selection is sent to all Mixer tracks
The selection is converted to MIDI notes
The selection is saved as a new pattern
music-production-083.e: The command creates an Audio Clip from the selected part or the whole sample.

music-production-087.p: Why are buffer underruns normally not heard in an offline export from FL Studio?
o: Rendering does not need to keep up with real time
Larger buffer, but still real time
Export takes place at a lower sample rate
music-production-087.e: In offline rendering the computer can take the time it needs on each block of audio.

music-production-088.p: What does Ctrl+L normally do to selected channels in FL Studio?
o: Routes them to free Mixer tracks
Puts a limiter on the Master
music-production-088.e: Ctrl+L connects selected Channel Rack channels to free Mixer tracks.

music-production-092.p: What is the purpose of Consolidate clips in FL Studio's Playlist?
o: To render the area to a new Audio Clip
To gather all plug-ins in one folder
To merge MIDI channels without audio
To reset automation in the area
music-production-092.e: Consolidation can be used to bounce or freeze an area as audio.

music-production-093.e: LUFS weights the signal according to human hearing and is used to describe perceived loudness.

music-production-094.p: What is the special purpose of a true-peak meter?
o: To find the project's root note
To measure MIDI velocity before recording
To show the reverb time of a room
music-production-094.e: True peak can reveal intersample peaks that an ordinary sample-peak meter may miss.

music-production-095.p: What is a de-esser designed to reduce?
o: Harsh s and sh sounds in vocals
music-production-095.e: A de-esser typically compresses a limited high-frequency range when sibilance becomes too strong.

music-production-100.p: Why do some plug-ins use oversampling?
o: To make mono into true stereo
To set the tempo more precisely
music-production-100.e: Oversampling works internally at a higher sample rate, but normally uses more CPU.

music-production-101.p: What are a room's standing waves?
music-production-101.e: Standing waves can cause strong peaks and dips, especially in the low-frequency response.

music-production-102.p: What does a signal's noise floor describe?
o: The level of the underlying noise
The distance between two MIDI notes
music-production-102.e: The noise floor is the basic level of noise from equipment, the room and electronics, among other things.

expansion-004.e: Vitamin K is involved in the formation of several clotting factors.

expansion-005.e: Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen in the lungs.

expansion-006.p: Which part of the brain especially helps with balance and coordination?
expansion-006.e: The cerebellum fine-tunes movements and contributes to balance.

expansion-007.p: What is the body's largest artery called?
expansion-007.e: The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle out into the body.

expansion-008.p: Which organs filter the blood and form urine?
expansion-008.e: The nephrons of the kidneys regulate fluid, salts and waste products, among other things.

expansion-009.p: What is a pulse a measure of?
expansion-009.e: The pulse normally follows the number of heart contractions.

expansion-010.p: Which cell type especially helps fight infections?
expansion-010.e: White blood cells include several types of immune cells.

o: A general rise in the price level
A surplus in the state budget
expansion-011.e: Inflation means that the purchasing power of money typically falls over time.

expansion-014.e: The issuer borrows capital and normally promises interest and repayment.

expansion-015.p: What does gross domestic product (GDP) measure?
o: The value of a country's production
expansion-015.e: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced in a period.

expansion-017.p: What does liquidity mean for an asset?
o: How easily it can be turned into money
expansion-017.e: Cash is highly liquid, while property, for example, takes longer to sell.

expansion-019.e: A deficit normally has to be financed by savings or borrowing.

expansion-024.e: Wind is renewed naturally and is not consumed like a fuel stock.

expansion-029.e: Microplastics are typically plastic particles smaller than five millimetres.

expansion-031.p: Which engine part ignites the mixture in a petrol engine?
expansion-031.e: The spark plug creates a spark in the combustion chamber.

expansion-034.e: ABS prevents the wheels from locking during hard braking.

expansion-039.p: In addition to kilowatts, what is a car's engine output often measured in?
expansion-039.e: Horsepower is an older, still widely used unit of power.

expansion-040.p: What does a vehicle's wheelbase indicate?
o: The distance between the front and rear axles
The overall width of the car
The ground clearance under the engine
expansion-040.e: The wheelbase affects, among other things, cabin space and handling.

expansion-041.p: Who designed the Sydney Opera House?
expansion-041.e: The Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the competition for the Opera House.

expansion-044.p: Which style is associated with pointed arches and flying buttresses?
expansion-044.e: Gothic cathedrals use these structures to support tall walls and large windows.

expansion-045.p: What does ergonomics mean in design?
o: Adapting to human use and the body
expansion-045.e: Ergonomics seeks to make products and environments safe and comfortable to use.

expansion-047.p: Which material is an alloy of iron and carbon?
expansion-047.e: The carbon content and treatment give steel different properties.

expansion-054.p: Which tool is used to check whether something is level?
expansion-054.e: The bubble in the spirit level's liquid-filled vial shows the slope.

expansion-055.p: What does the symbol of three arrows in a triangle mean?
expansion-055.e: The Möbius loop is used internationally as the recycling symbol.

expansion-062.p: Which Danish city is known for Den Gamle By?
expansion-062.e: Den Gamle By is an open-air museum in the middle of Aarhus.

expansion-063.p: What is the Folketing's (the Danish parliament's) control of the government based on, among other things?
expansion-063.e: A government must not have a majority against it in the Folketing.

expansion-064.p: Who signs a passed Danish law together with a minister?
o: The President of the Supreme Court
expansion-064.e: The Danish Constitution requires royal assent and the countersignature of a minister.

expansion-065.p: Which organisation has the General Assembly and the Security Council?
expansion-065.e: Both bodies are central parts of the United Nations.

expansion-066.p: Where is the European Parliament's official seat?
expansion-066.e: Parliament holds its plenary sessions in Strasbourg, although much of the work takes place in Brussels.

expansion-067.e: Cuneiform arose in Mesopotamia and was pressed into clay tablets.

expansion-068.p: Which event triggered the First World War?
expansion-068.e: The murder of Archduke Franz Ferdinand triggered the crisis in 1914.

expansion-069.p: What is the term for the direct transition from solid to gas?
expansion-069.e: Dry ice sublimates at normal atmospheric pressure.

expansion-070.p: Which cell part contains most of the human DNA?
expansion-070.e: Most of the chromosomes are located in the cell nucleus.

expansion-073.p: Which philosopher is associated with virtue ethics?
expansion-073.e: Aristotle emphasised character virtues and the good life.

expansion-077.p: Who is associated with social learning theory and the Bobo doll studies?
expansion-077.e: Bandura showed the importance of observation and modelling.

expansion-079.e: The novel follows Josef K. through an impenetrable legal system.

expansion-080.e: The Belgian detective appears in several of Christie's crime novels.

expansion-081.e: The novel about meaning and peer pressure was published in 2000.

expansion-082.e: J.P. Jacobsen's historical novel was published in 1876.

expansion-083.e: The Celebration (Festen) from 1998 was the first Dogme 95 film.

expansion-085.p: Which Danish series follows employees at the pharmaceutical company SanaFortis?
expansion-085.e: Lykke follows working life and relationships at the pharmaceutical company SanaFortis.

expansion-086.p: Who plays Sarah Lund in The Killing?
expansion-086.e: Sarah Lund's knitted jumper became a well-known visual trademark of the series.

expansion-089.p: In which sport is the term birdie used?
expansion-089.e: A birdie is one stroke under the par of the hole.

expansion-090.p: In which sport is a slam dunk performed?
expansion-090.e: In a slam dunk, the ball is pushed straight down through the hoop with the hand.

expansion-091.p: Who won the Tour de France in 1996?
expansion-091.e: Bjarne Riis became the first Danish overall winner.

expansion-092.p: Which Danish badminton player won Olympic gold in men's singles in Tokyo?
expansion-092.e: Viktor Axelsen won the final at the postponed Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

expansion-094.p: Which card means a player is sent off in football?
expansion-094.e: A direct red card sends the player off for the rest of the match.

expansion-095.e: The platypus is a monotreme and combines egg-laying with milk production.

expansion-096.p: What do sharks especially use the lateral line system for?
expansion-096.e: The sensory organ detects vibrations and pressure changes.

expansion-097.p: Which Nordic animal often changes its fur colour to white in winter?
expansion-097.e: Many Arctic foxes grow white winter fur as camouflage in snow.

expansion-099.p: Which deciduous tree has smooth grey bark and is Denmark's national tree?
expansion-099.e: The beech thrives in Denmark's mild, humid climate.

expansion-103.p: Who is the father of Fenrir in Norse mythology?
expansion-103.e: Fenrir is one of Loki's children, together with the giantess Angrboda.

expansion-104.e: Heimdall has keen senses and announces Ragnarok with the Gjallarhorn.

expansion-106.p: Which toy brand has minifigures with distinctive yellow heads?
expansion-106.e: The LEGO minifigure was introduced in its modern form in 1978.

expansion-107.p: Which company is behind the Android operating system?
expansion-107.e: Google bought Android Inc. and develops the platform with the Open Handset Alliance.

expansion-111.p: What are Finnish karjalanpiirakka traditionally often filled with?
expansion-111.e: Karelian pasties have a thin rye crust and are often filled with rice porridge.

expansion-116.p: What does a classic Negroni consist of in equal parts?
expansion-116.e: The Negroni is a bitter Italian aperitif cocktail.

expansion-119.p: Which digital pet craze was launched in the 1990s?
expansion-119.e: The Tamagotchi came from Bandai and required constant digital care.

expansion-120.p: What was the name of the cloned sheep born in 1996?
expansion-120.e: Dolly was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell.

expansion-121.p: What is the idea that an action is right if it creates the greatest possible overall benefit called?
expansion-121.e: Utilitarianism judges actions by their consequences for overall welfare.

expansion-126.p: Which house does Luna Lovegood belong to?
expansion-126.e: Luna is a Ravenclaw student and known for her curiosity and unconventional thinking.

expansion-127.p: What is the wizard bank in the Harry Potter universe called?
expansion-127.e: Gringotts is run by goblins and is located on Diagon Alley.

expansion-128.p: What kind of owl is Harry Potter's Hedwig?
expansion-128.e: Hedwig is a white snowy owl and Harry's post owl.

expansion-130.p: What does the Marauder's Map show?
o: The family tree of the Black family
expansion-130.e: The map shows the castle's corridors and named people moving about.

expansion-133.p: Which stage layout has the audience all the way around the playing area?
expansion-133.e: On an arena stage the performance is seen from several directions.

expansion-136.p: Which female scientist received Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry?
expansion-136.e: Marie Curie was honoured for her work on radioactivity and the discovery of new elements.

expansion-138.p: Who developed the first published algorithm intended for a machine?
expansion-138.e: Lovelace described an algorithm for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.

expansion-139.p: Which naturalist formulated evolution by natural selection?
expansion-139.e: Darwin gathered extensive evidence for the gradual change of species.

expansion-140.p: Who was the first human in space?
expansion-140.e: Gagarin orbited the Earth in Vostok 1 in 1961.

expansion-153.p: Which statement is correct about sound in a vacuum?
o: Sound travels fastest in a vacuum
Only bass tones can be heard
expansion-153.e: Mechanical sound waves require matter that can vibrate.

expansion-154.p: Which statement is correct about Venus?
o: It rotates in the opposite direction to most planets
It is the most distant planet from the Sun
expansion-154.e: Venus has retrograde rotation and no natural moons.

expansion-163.p: Which space shuttle was lost during re-entry in 2003?
expansion-163.e: The Columbia disaster cost all seven astronauts on board their lives.

expansion-166.p: Which rover landed on Mars in 2012?
expansion-166.e: Curiosity was lowered down using a so-called sky crane in Gale Crater.

expansion-169.p: Which Danish TV series about politics achieved international success in the 2010s?
expansion-169.e: Borgen follows Birgitte Nyborg and Danish power politics.

expansion-170.p: Which music service was listed on the stock exchange in 2018?
expansion-170.e: Spotify chose a direct listing on the New York Stock Exchange.

curiosity-001.p: Why does road salt help against ice on the road?
o: It lowers the freezing point of water
It sucks the ice down into the road
It makes the ice evaporate immediately
curiosity-001.e: When salt dissolves in the water on the ice's surface, brine forms, which freezes at a lower temperature than pure water.

curiosity-002.p: A metal railing and a wooden railing are at the same temperature. Why does the metal feel coldest?
o: Wood fibres hold on to the heat
curiosity-002.e: The sensation of cold depends on how quickly the skin loses heat. Metal conducts heat far better than wood.

curiosity-003.p: Why does a clear daytime sky look blue?
o: The air scatters blue light the most
The sun emits the most blue light
curiosity-003.e: Short-wavelength blue light is scattered more in the atmosphere than longer-wavelength red light. The phenomenon is called Rayleigh scattering.

curiosity-004.p: Why does the sunset often turn red or orange?
o: The sea colours the clouds from below
Earth's magnetic field filters the colours
curiosity-004.e: At sunset, light has a longer path through the atmosphere. Much of the blue light is scattered away, while the red tones get through.

curiosity-005.p: What property makes ice cubes float in a glass of water?
o: Ice has a lower density than water
Surface tension carries the ice cube
Cold water pushes the ice upwards
curiosity-005.e: When water freezes, the molecules form an open crystal structure. Therefore ice takes up more space and has a lower density than water.

curiosity-006.p: Why do stars twinkle more than planets seen from Earth?
o: Point light is affected by turbulent air
curiosity-006.e: A star is seen almost as a single point of light, which is easily affected by turbulent air. A planet's small disc evens out much of the flickering.

curiosity-007.p: Why do you see lightning before you hear thunder?
o: Light is far faster than sound
The eye reacts faster than the ear
curiosity-007.e: Light reaches us practically instantly over short distances, while sound travels through air at about 343 metres per second.

curiosity-010.p: Where does the water on the outside of a cold glass come from?
o: Water vapour in the air condenses
The cold draws liquid up from the table
curiosity-010.e: The cold surface of the glass cools the air close to it. When the air reaches its dew point, water vapour gathers as droplets.

curiosity-011.p: Why does a bathroom mirror steam up after a hot shower?
o: Vapour condenses on the cold glass
The glass sucks moisture from the wall
The mirror's metal coating releases droplets
curiosity-011.e: The humid air cools at the mirror, and the water vapour turns into microscopic droplets that make the surface cloudy.

curiosity-012.p: Why do you get small static electric shocks more often in winter?
o: Dry air carries charge away poorly
Winter clothing carries charge away faster
Indoor air adds charge to the body
curiosity-012.e: In low humidity, charge tends to stay on the body. Humid air helps it drain away continuously.

curiosity-013.p: What is the main cause of the seasons on Earth?
o: The tilt of Earth's axis towards the Sun
The Sun's energy varies every half year
curiosity-013.e: The axial tilt changes both the angle of sunlight and the length of the day. In fact, Earth is closest to the Sun during the northern hemisphere's winter.

curiosity-014.p: Why does the Moon almost always show the same side to Earth?
o: Its rotation and orbit take the same time
The far side is heaviest and turns away
The Moon does not rotate at all
Earth's shadow hides the far side
curiosity-014.e: The Moon is tidally locked: it takes roughly the same time to rotate once as to orbit Earth once.

curiosity-015.p: Why is sea water salty, when rain and most rivers do not taste salty?
o: Waves turn stones into table salt
Salt on the seabed dissolves quickly
curiosity-015.e: Water dissolves small amounts of minerals from rock and soil. Rivers carry the ions to the sea, while evaporation removes water but not the salt.

curiosity-016.p: How does soap help remove grease from a plate?
o: Soap binds both grease and water
curiosity-016.e: Soap molecules have a water-loving end and a grease-loving end. They surround the grease so that it can be rinsed away with the water.

curiosity-017.p: What makes your eyes water when you cut onions?
o: The scent dries out the tear ducts
curiosity-017.e: When onion cells are damaged, a volatile irritant is formed. Tears try to dilute the substance and wash it away.

curiosity-018.p: Why does a cut apple turn brown?
o: Enzymes react with oxygen in the air
The apple absorbs colour from the seeds
The water in the apple turns to rust
curiosity-018.e: When the cells are cut open, enzymes and phenolic compounds meet oxygen. This forms brown pigments.

curiosity-019.p: Why can lemon juice slow down the browning of a cut apple?
o: Lemon permanently closes the apple's pores
Lemon juice turns the apple white
The sugar in the lemon freezes the surface
curiosity-019.e: The low pH inhibits the browning enzyme, and vitamin C can react with oxidising substances before the apple's tissue does.

curiosity-021.p: What makes a corn kernel burst like popcorn?
o: Water in the kernel turns into steam
Air in the kernel bursts the husk
curiosity-021.e: The hard shell holds the steam in until the pressure becomes high enough. Then the shell breaks, and the soft starch expands.

curiosity-022.p: Why does an egg become solid when it is boiled?
o: The proteins form a firm network
Water is pressed out through the shell's pores
The yolk soaks up fat from the white
The shell squeezes the contents together
curiosity-022.e: The heat denatures the egg's proteins. The unfolded proteins form a network that makes the white and yolk firm.

curiosity-023.p: What causes bubbles to form when a soda bottle is opened?
o: A drop in pressure releases dissolved carbon dioxide
Air draws CO₂ out of the liquid
Oxygen reacts with CO₂ and forms foam
curiosity-023.e: Under pressure, more carbon dioxide can be dissolved in the soda. When the bottle is opened, the pressure falls and the gas escapes as bubbles.

curiosity-024.p: What does it normally mean when liquid honey crystallises?
o: All the water has turned into sugar
Beeswax has melted into the honey
curiosity-024.e: Crystallisation is a natural process and does not mean that the honey has gone off. The ratio of glucose to water affects the speed.

curiosity-025.p: Why does chilli feel hot, even though the food is not particularly hot?
o: The spice warms the mucous membrane
The acid in the chilli activates pain nerves
The red colour fools the brain
curiosity-025.e: Capsaicin binds to the TRPV1 receptor, which normally responds to high temperature and tissue damage. The brain interprets the signal as heat.

curiosity-026.p: Why does menthol feel cool in the mouth?
o: It evaporates and cools the mouth
It restricts blood flow to the tongue
curiosity-026.e: Menthol affects, among others, the TRPM8 receptor, which also responds to cold. The temperature does not actually have to drop.

curiosity-028.p: Why does a double-glazed window insulate better than a single thick pane?
o: Air between the panes slows the heat
The glass reflects the heat back
Two thin panes conduct less heat
Pressure between the panes keeps it warm
curiosity-028.e: Still air or an insulating gas between the panes conducts heat worse than glass and limits air circulation.

curiosity-029.p: Why are radiators often placed under windows?
o: The glass amplifies the radiator's heat
curiosity-029.e: Air cooled by the window sinks. The radiator warms it and creates a circulation that reduces draughts and temperature differences.

curiosity-030.p: Why do long bridges have movable joints?
o: The material changes length with heat
The gaps dampen vibrations from traffic
curiosity-030.e: Steel and concrete change length when the temperature changes. The joints allow room for the movement and prevent cracks and deformation.

curiosity-031.p: Why doesn't a bird normally get an electric shock when it sits on a single power line?
o: Its feet have almost the same voltage
Its feathers insulate it from current
The bird's weight cuts off the current
The current runs along the underside of the wire
curiosity-031.e: Current through the body requires a difference in voltage. The danger arises if the bird simultaneously touches another voltage or the earth.

curiosity-032.p: What is the purpose of an electrical fuse that melts?
curiosity-032.e: Too much current heats the fuse wire until it melts and breaks the circuit. This protects wires from overheating and fire.

curiosity-033.p: What happens to a room if a fridge is left open and running for a long time?
o: The air is cooled, the walls are not
curiosity-033.e: The fridge moves heat, and it releases both the moved heat and the extra energy from the compressor into the room. That is why the room ends up warmer.

curiosity-034.p: Why does a fan cool a person but not an empty closed room?
o: Airflow increases evaporation from the skin
The body draws in the motor's heat
The air loses energy by moving
curiosity-034.e: A fan moves air and helps sweat evaporate. In an empty room, the motor actually adds a small amount of heat.

curiosity-035.p: Why does the turntable rotate in many microwave ovens?
o: Food is moved through uneven fields
The turntable blows hot air around
The movement keeps the water in the food
curiosity-035.e: Microwaves create an uneven pattern of energy inside the oven. Rotation spreads the food between hotter and cooler areas.

curiosity-036.p: Why can a phone battery perform worse in severe cold?
o: The chemistry in the battery slows down
The screen uses power on the glass
curiosity-036.e: Low temperature increases the battery's internal resistance and slows the reaction rate. The capacity often returns when the battery warms up again.

curiosity-037.p: Why does a car's tyre pressure often drop in cold weather?
o: The air in the tyre contracts
The road sucks air through the tread
curiosity-037.e: When a fixed quantity of gas becomes colder, the molecules move more slowly and the pressure falls.

curiosity-038.p: Why can full-beam headlights make it harder to see in dense fog?
o: The droplets scatter the light back
The vapour absorbs the headlights' red light
The beam heats up the fog
curiosity-038.e: The bright light hits many tiny water droplets and is scattered. A large part comes back as a bright veil in front of the car.

curiosity-039.p: How do reflectors on road signs make them clear in the dark?
o: Small prisms reflect the light back
Wind pressure creates power in the sign
curiosity-039.e: Retroreflective material sends light back roughly in the direction it came from, so the car's headlights send the light back towards the driver.

curiosity-040.p: What is the main job of a tyre's tread on a wet road?
o: To channel water away from the contact patch
To heat the asphalt under the car
To make the tyre heavier at high speed
To soak up the water in the rubber
curiosity-040.e: The grooves give the water a path away, so the rubber can maintain better contact with the road and resist aquaplaning.

curiosity-041.p: Why can your ears feel blocked during take-off and landing in an aeroplane?
o: The engines suck air out of the ear
curiosity-041.e: The Eustachian tube must equalise the pressure between the middle ear and the surroundings. Swallowing or yawning can help the tube open.

curiosity-042.p: Why are the windows in passenger aeroplanes rounded at the corners?
o: A round shape distributes pressure better
They are easier to open in an emergency
curiosity-042.e: Sharp corners concentrate mechanical stress and can start cracks. Rounded windows spread the load from the cabin pressure.

curiosity-043.p: Why does Wi-Fi often get weaker through a thick concrete wall?
o: Concrete uses the signal as power
The router cannot measure the room
The network stops at grey surfaces
curiosity-043.e: Water, metal and dense building materials can absorb or reflect radio waves. Reinforcing steel in concrete can dampen the signal further.

curiosity-044.p: Why does satellite navigation often work worse inside large buildings?
o: The building dampens the weak signals
The signals become imprecise when stationary
The phone needs a compass pointing north
curiosity-044.e: Navigation signals come from satellites far away and are very weak at Earth's surface. Roofs, walls and metal can block or reflect them.

curiosity-045.p: How can a QR code often be read even when a small part is damaged?
o: The camera guesses from the edges
The damage is replaced from a database
curiosity-045.e: QR codes use error correction, so missing or unreadable parts can be reconstructed to a certain extent.

curiosity-046.p: What does private or incognito browsing normally not hide?
o: The network owner can see the traffic
Websites cannot see your IP address
The provider sees only encrypted domains
curiosity-046.e: Private browsing mainly limits traces on the device itself. The network, the services visited and any employer can still record connections.

curiosity-047.p: What does the SPF number on sun cream mainly tell you?
o: How long the cream is water-resistant
curiosity-047.e: SPF is a measure linked to UVB protection under standardised conditions. The effect also depends on the amount applied, water and reapplication.

curiosity-048.p: Why does a mosquito bite itch?
o: The immune system reacts to the saliva
The mosquito leaves a hair behind
The blood clots and becomes warm
curiosity-048.e: The mosquito's saliva helps it suck blood. The body's immune reaction releases histamine, among other things, which causes swelling and itching.

curiosity-049.p: Why does a bruise change colour while it heals?
curiosity-049.e: When blood outside the blood vessels is cleared away, haemoglobin breaks down into different coloured substances. That is why the bruise can turn purple, green and yellowish.

curiosity-050.p: What were goose bumps originally useful for in animals with fur?
o: Hair stands up and insulates with air
Pores close to make it waterproof
curiosity-050.e: Small muscles raise the hairs. In animals, this can both insulate and make the animal look bigger; in humans the effect is modest.

curiosity-051.p: What happens during an ordinary hiccup?
curiosity-051.e: A sudden contraction of the diaphragm is followed by the vocal cords closing. This creates the characteristic sound.

curiosity-052.p: What mainly contributes to the distinctive smell of rain on dry soil?
curiosity-052.e: Raindrops can release aerosols containing, among other things, geosmin from soil bacteria and plant oils. The smell is often called petrichor.

curiosity-053.p: Why do most clouds look white, even though water is transparent?
o: Ice crystals filter out dark colours
curiosity-053.e: The many droplets and ice crystals scatter visible light in all colours. The colours mix and are perceived as white or grey.

curiosity-054.p: Why does a black jumper often get warmer in direct sun than a white one?
curiosity-054.e: Dark surfaces typically absorb more of the incoming light, while light surfaces reflect a greater proportion.

curiosity-expansion-001.p: Why can you see your breath on a cold day?
o: Water vapour turns into tiny droplets
The cold freezes small droplets from the mouth
The lungs release more water in the cold
Warm air makes dust in the air visible
curiosity-expansion-001.e: Exhaled air is warm and humid. In the cold air, some of the water vapour condenses into tiny droplets that scatter the light.

curiosity-expansion-002.p: Why does warm air usually rise?
o: It is less dense than cold air
It has more oxygen and is pulled upwards
The pressure beneath it is lower
curiosity-expansion-002.e: When air is heated, it expands. The same amount of air fills more space and thus has a lower density than the cooler air around it.

curiosity-expansion-003.p: Why can a spoon look bent in a glass of water?
o: Light changes direction in the water
The water magnifies only the bottom
The eye swaps light and shadow
curiosity-expansion-003.e: Light travels at different speeds in air and water, so it is refracted at the boundary. The eye interprets the rays as if they came straight.

curiosity-expansion-004.p: Why does the air feel cooler when it is windy?
o: The warm layer of air is blown away
Cold air is pressed into the skin
Movement lowers the temperature of the air
curiosity-expansion-004.e: The skin warms a thin layer of air. The wind continuously replaces it with cooler air and at the same time increases evaporation from the skin.

curiosity-expansion-005.p: Why can ordinary sound barely travel in outer space?
o: There is no matter for the sound waves
The cold makes sound waves too slow
The sun drowns out all vibrations
Weak gravity bends the sound away
curiosity-expansion-005.e: Sound consists of mechanical vibrations and requires a medium such as air, water or metal. The almost empty space therefore cannot carry ordinary sound waves.

curiosity-expansion-006.p: Why do astronauts float in a space station?
o: They are in constant free fall
There is no gravity up there
The air in the station lifts them
curiosity-expansion-006.e: Gravity is still strong in low Earth orbit. Astronauts experience weightlessness because they and the station are in constant free fall around the Earth.

curiosity-expansion-007.p: Why does the Moon look larger close to the horizon?
o: The atmosphere acts like a lens
The Moon is closest at the horizon
The retina magnifies light near the ground
curiosity-expansion-007.e: The lunar disc occupies roughly the same visual angle high and low in the sky. The impression of size at the horizon is mainly an optical illusion.

curiosity-expansion-008.p: Why do fingers become wrinkled after a long time in water?
o: The skin soaks up water and swells unevenly
Water pressure presses the tissue in
Cold makes the fat layer shrink
curiosity-expansion-008.e: The wrinkling is an active reaction controlled by the nerves, not merely absorbed water. A possible benefit is a better grip on wet objects.

curiosity-expansion-009.p: Why does your nose often run when you eat hot chilli?
o: Heat dilates the blood vessels in the nose
Spicy food increases pressure in the sinuses
curiosity-expansion-009.e: Capsaicin activates some of the same receptors as heat and irritation. The body responds with more mucus and tears, among other things.

curiosity-expansion-010.p: Why does it hurt to eat ice cream very quickly?
o: Blood vessels in the palate constrict
Cold stimulates the nerves of the teeth
The palate gets a cold cramp
The pressure in the sinuses falls
curiosity-expansion-010.e: The rapid cooling and subsequent dilation of blood vessels around the palate activate pain pathways. The pain is often felt in the forehead.

curiosity-expansion-011.p: Why are you more likely to yawn when others yawn?
o: The sound activates the jaw's stretch reflex
Yawning lowers the oxygen level in the room
The face makes the eyes dry out
curiosity-expansion-011.e: Contagious yawning is linked to social attention and the brain's tendency to automatically imitate actions. The precise function is still debated.

curiosity-expansion-012.p: Why does one nostril often get more blocked than the other?
o: The nasal mucosa follows a nasal cycle
The lungs use one nostril at a time
curiosity-expansion-012.e: The so-called nasal cycle is controlled automatically. The tissue alternately swells in each nostril over several hours, without you normally noticing.

curiosity-expansion-013.p: Why does waiting often feel longer when you don't know how long it will last?
o: Stress speeds up the brain's clock
Unknown time is stored as more memories
curiosity-expansion-013.e: When the end point is unclear, we pay more attention to time and lack a sense of control. Information about how long the wait will be can make it more tolerable.

curiosity-expansion-014.p: Why do people often remember the beginning and end of a list best?
o: Start and end each have an advantage
The eye reads the extremes slowly
The middle is confused with other items
curiosity-expansion-014.e: The first items reach long-term memory more easily, while the last ones are still fresh in working memory. This is called the primacy and recency effect.

curiosity-expansion-015.p: Why can a song keep running through your head?
o: The brain repeats a simple pattern
The hair cells in the ear keep vibrating
The tempo takes over the brain's rhythm
curiosity-expansion-015.e: An earworm is an involuntary musical memory. Repetition, a simple melody and interrupted pieces of music can make it more persistent.

curiosity-expansion-016.p: A freshly kneaded bread dough shrinks back while being shaped. Why does a short rest help?
o: The yeast stops and the dough sets
The starch sets and holds its shape
The salt breaks down the gluten proteins
curiosity-expansion-016.e: Kneading stretches the gluten network. During the rest, moisture is distributed and the gluten becomes more pliable, so the dough can be shaped without springing back.

curiosity-expansion-017.p: Why is a freshly baked biscuit often soft but becomes crisp as it cools?
curiosity-expansion-017.e: In the warm biscuit, the fat and sugar are still soft, and there is more steam in the structure. As it cools, it sets while some moisture escapes.

curiosity-expansion-018.p: Why can a cake collapse if the oven door is opened too early?
o: The structure is too weak for the gas
The steam escapes through the surface
curiosity-expansion-018.e: Early in baking, gas and steam expand the dough, but the proteins and starch have not yet set. A drop in temperature can therefore cause the structure to collapse.

curiosity-expansion-019.p: Why do tomatoes often taste stronger at room temperature than straight from the fridge?
o: Cold binds the acid to the flesh
The fridge breaks down the sugar
curiosity-expansion-019.e: Taste depends heavily on smell. At room temperature more volatile aroma compounds are released, so the nose registers a more intense flavour.

curiosity-expansion-020.p: Why does cooked pasta stick together more when it cools without sauce?
o: The starch on the surface becomes sticky
curiosity-expansion-020.e: During cooking, starch is released to the surface. When the moisture evaporates and the pasta stands still, the sticky starch can make the pieces cling together.

curiosity-expansion-021.p: Why does an avocado turn brown after it has been cut?
o: Enzymes react with oxygen in the air
The stone releases a brown dye
The fruit loses all its water
curiosity-expansion-021.e: When the cells are damaged, enzymes and plant compounds meet oxygen. The reaction forms brown pigments and can be slowed by acid or less contact with air.

curiosity-expansion-022.p: How can pickling extend the shelf life of food?
o: Acid, salt and sugar inhibit microbes
The jar removes oxygen and sterilises the food
The glass dries the food from the inside
curiosity-expansion-022.e: A low pH and a high concentration of salt or sugar make the environment harder for many microorganisms. Clean storage and correct heat treatment are also important.

curiosity-expansion-023.p: Why are some cocktails served with one large ice cube rather than many small ones?
o: Large ice is denser and keeps cold longer
curiosity-expansion-023.e: A large ice cube typically melts more slowly relative to its mass, so it dilutes the drink more slowly once it has become cold.

curiosity-expansion-024.p: Why can sparkling wine foam violently after being shaken?
o: Shaking creates nucleation sites for bubbles
Air is pressed down through the cork
curiosity-expansion-024.e: Shaking distributes small gas pockets in the liquid. When the pressure drops on opening, the bubbles grow quickly and push liquid out.

curiosity-expansion-025.p: Why does a computer often slow down when its working memory is almost full?
o: Data is moved between RAM and disk
The processor slows down to spare RAM
curiosity-expansion-025.e: When RAM runs short, the system can use the SSD or hard disk as temporary memory. This is far slower than retrieving data directly from RAM.

curiosity-expansion-026.p: Why does a phone get hot during a demanding game?
o: The chip's work gives off heat
The speaker sucks in hot air
curiosity-expansion-026.e: Billions of transistors switch state many times a second. Part of the electrical energy ends up as heat in the chip and battery.

curiosity-expansion-027.p: Why can noise-cancelling headphones reduce engine drone?
o: Anti-phase waves partly cancel sound waves
The cushions move noise above the hearing threshold
The microphone filters the sound out of the ear
curiosity-expansion-027.e: Microphones measure the surrounding sound, and the headphones produce roughly the opposite wave. The method works especially well on steady, low-frequency noise.

curiosity-expansion-028.p: Why does a phone charge more slowly when close to 100 per cent?
o: The current is reduced to spare the battery
The last percentages are physically larger
The socket runs out of voltage
The screen uses the power after 80 per cent
curiosity-expansion-028.e: Lithium-ion batteries charge quickly at first, but the electronics reduce the current near full charge to limit heat and stress.

curiosity-expansion-029.p: How can a website remember a shopping basket without a login?
o: The browser stores a local ID
The site recognises the screen resolution
The search engine stores a copy
curiosity-expansion-029.e: A website can use, for example, a cookie or local storage to link the browser to a temporary basket.

curiosity-expansion-030.p: Why can a message still arrive when the internet does not choose one fixed route?
o: Data is split into packets that find their way
All messages go via one satellite
The recipient fetches it from the sender's screen
Routers copy the network every minute
curiosity-expansion-030.e: The internet is a packet-switched network. Routers forward data packets step by step, and the recipient reassembles them.

curiosity-expansion-031.p: Why do many web addresses begin with HTTPS?
o: The browser has fact-checked the site
The server is in the same country
The address is hidden from the provider
curiosity-expansion-031.e: HTTPS uses encryption and certificates to protect the connection. It does not guarantee that the site's content or owner is trustworthy.

curiosity-expansion-032.p: Why can a video start before the whole file has been downloaded?
o: The server sends the ending first
Sound is stored locally, the picture is streamed
curiosity-expansion-032.e: Streaming sends the content in smaller pieces. A short buffer gives the player data to show while the rest continues to download.

curiosity-expansion-034.p: Why can two almost identical tones create a slow pulsing sound?
o: The waves reinforce and cancel each other
The ear switches between the pitches
The low tone modulates the speaker
curiosity-expansion-034.e: The difference between the frequencies creates beats. If the tones are, for example, 440 and 443 Hz, you hear roughly three pulses per second.

curiosity-expansion-035.p: Why should a sound mix also be tested at low volume?
o: It makes all frequencies equally clear
It shows the mix after data compression
It removes the influence of the room
curiosity-expansion-035.e: At low volume, the hierarchy of the mix becomes clear: important parts should still be audible. The ear is also less sensitive to very low and very high frequencies.

curiosity-expansion-036.p: Why can too much compression make music sound flat?
o: The difference between loud and quiet is reduced
High frequencies are damped the most
The stereo image collapses into the middle
curiosity-expansion-036.e: A compressor reduces dynamic range. Used heavily, it can remove the contrast and movement between hits, verses and choruses.

curiosity-expansion-037.p: Why is a crossfade used between two edited pieces of audio?
o: The transition becomes smooth without a click
curiosity-expansion-037.e: A sudden change in the waveform can cause a click. A short crossfade lowers one clip while raising the other, so the transition is smoother.

curiosity-expansion-038.p: What makes a dog's shake so effective at removing water?
o: Fast rotation gives the droplets speed
Hair channels water out by capillary action
Body heat evaporates the water quickly
curiosity-expansion-038.e: The dog's skin and fur quickly change direction during the shake. The droplets cannot follow the movement and are flung off; this takes far less energy than evaporating the water.

curiosity-expansion-039.p: Why does a cat often land on its paws after a fall?
o: It turns the front and back of its body in opposite directions
The tail pulls the centre of gravity down
The paws are heavier than the rest
The fur gives lift under the belly
curiosity-expansion-039.e: The cat uses its flexible spine and changes how the front and back halves rotate. It can therefore turn over without having anything to push against.

curiosity-expansion-040.p: Why do flamingos often stand on one leg?
o: The posture needs little muscular effort
The other leg cannot tolerate water
They change legs against the wind
One leg makes them invisible to fish
curiosity-expansion-040.e: The flamingo's joints can stabilise the body on one leg with modest muscular effort. The posture can also reduce heat loss in cold water.

curiosity-expansion-041.p: Why does a mosquito buzz close to your ear?
o: The wing beats create audible pressure waves
The mosquito calls out to humans
The proboscis works like a whistle
The ear amplifies the mosquito's breathing
curiosity-expansion-041.e: A mosquito's wings beat hundreds of times a second. The frequency lies in the audible range and is clearly noticeable when the insect is close to the ear.

curiosity-expansion-042.p: Why do many conifers keep their needles in winter?
o: The needles reduce water loss and tolerate frost
Wax makes photosynthesis better in frost
The resin carries heat to the needles
The narrow shape makes snow turn into water
curiosity-expansion-042.e: Needles have a small surface area, a waxy skin and other adaptations that reduce water loss. The tree can therefore keep them for several years.

curiosity-expansion-043.p: Why is moss often more widespread in damp, shady places?
o: It dries out more slowly there
curiosity-expansion-043.e: Moss has no roots or transport system like larger plants and absorbs water across its surface. It therefore often thrives where moisture lasts longer.

curiosity-expansion-044.p: Why can a forest be cooler than an open area in summer?
o: Trees provide shade and evaporate water
Leaves absorb all the warm air
curiosity-expansion-044.e: The canopy limits the sunlight reaching the ground, and evaporation from the leaves uses energy. Together these can lower the temperature locally.

curiosity-expansion-045.p: Why do city centres often become warmer than the areas around them?
o: Tall houses are closer to the Sun
curiosity-expansion-045.e: Dark roofs and surfaces absorb solar energy, buildings retain heat, and there are often fewer plants to cool through evaporation.

curiosity-expansion-046.p: Why can peat bogs store large amounts of carbon?
o: Moss turns CO₂ directly into peat
Water carries carbon down into the soil
curiosity-expansion-046.e: Waterlogged, oxygen-poor soil slows decomposition. Plant material and its carbon can therefore accumulate as peat over thousands of years.

curiosity-expansion-048.p: Why does condensation often form on the inside of a car windscreen in winter?
o: A cold windscreen cools moist air to dew point
Pressure differences push moisture through the glass
The hot air from the blower releases water
Cold air deposits moisture on the inside
curiosity-expansion-048.e: Passengers' breath and wet clothing add moisture. When the cabin air is cooled by the cold windscreen to below its dew point, the water vapour condenses on the glass.

curiosity-expansion-049.p: Why is a train more energy-efficient than many cars carrying the same number of passengers?
o: Low rolling resistance and shared air resistance
Electric motors have no energy loss
Weight is distributed directly into the ground
curiosity-expansion-049.e: Steel wheels on steel rails deform less than car tyres, and many passengers are moved in one long vehicle with relatively little air resistance per person.

curiosity-expansion-051.p: Why do tall buildings often have a heavy, moving mass near the top?
o: It can counteract the building's sway
It presses the foundations deeper down
It keeps the lifts in balance
curiosity-expansion-051.e: A tuned mass damper moves out of phase with the building and reduces unpleasant sway caused by wind or earthquakes.

curiosity-expansion-052.p: Why does a loan become more expensive when interest rates rise?
o: The bank adds interest on top of the debt
Repayments fall, so the loan runs longer
curiosity-expansion-052.e: Interest is the payment for using the lender's money. A higher interest rate means greater interest costs if the rest of the loan remains unchanged.

curiosity-expansion-054.p: Why does an investment fund typically spread its money across many securities?
o: All securities get the same return
Fluctuations even out at a minimum number of holdings
curiosity-expansion-054.e: Diversification reduces company-specific risk. It cannot remove market risk or guarantee a positive return.

curiosity-expansion-055.p: Why do related languages often have systematic similarities?
o: They have borrowed root words from one language
The same alphabet gives the same grammar
curiosity-expansion-055.e: Related languages are branches of a common ancestor. Regular sound changes can therefore be traced in words and grammar, even after a long period of separation.

curiosity-expansion-056.p: Why do words sometimes change meaning over history?
o: People use them differently over time
Spelling reforms give words a new definition
curiosity-expansion-056.e: Language is shaped by its users. Metaphors, technology, culture and repeated use can broaden, narrow or shift the meaning of a word.

curiosity-expansion-057.p: What is the main reading benefit of spaces between words?
o: Word boundaries are easier to see
They show where the stress lies
They keep the letter spacing even
curiosity-expansion-057.e: Clear word boundaries make words quicker to recognise. Ancient texts were often written without fixed spaces, which demanded more of the reader.

curiosity-expansion-058.p: Why is the climate of Western Europe milder than at the same latitude in parts of Canada?
o: Ocean currents and westerly winds warm it
Rotation gathers cold air in Canada
curiosity-expansion-058.e: The Atlantic stores and moves heat, partly via the North Atlantic current system. The westerly winds carry the maritime air over Europe.

curiosity-expansion-059.p: Why does air temperature typically fall with height in the troposphere?
o: Thin air absorbs less solar heat
Water vapour freezes and cools the air
curiosity-expansion-059.e: Air pressure falls with height. When rising air expands under the lower pressure, it uses energy and becomes cooler; the process is called adiabatic cooling.

curiosity-expansion-060.p: Why do time zones not always follow lines of longitude precisely?
o: Countries adapt time to practical needs
curiosity-expansion-060.e: Solar time changes gradually with longitude, but official time zones are set administratively and often follow national borders and economic ties.

curiosity-expansion-061.p: Why does a melody sound brighter when played faster from an analogue tape?
o: Only the low tones are erased
curiosity-expansion-061.e: When the tape moves faster, every vibration passes the playback head more quickly. Therefore both the pitch and the tempo rise.

curiosity-expansion-062.p: Which change can give a chorus more lift than the verse?
o: A lower key and shorter notes
The same arrangement at lower volume
curiosity-expansion-062.e: A chorus can be lifted with extra voices and instruments, a wider frequency range and more dynamic intensity. The contrast with the verse is crucial.

curiosity-expansion-063.p: Why can a football swerve in the air after an off-centre kick?
o: Seams pull towards the direction of the kick
curiosity-expansion-063.e: A rotating ball affects the airflow differently on each side. The Magnus effect produces a sideways force and a curved path.

curiosity-expansion-064.p: Why does a pole vaulter bend the pole during the jump?
o: It stores the energy of the run
The curve increases the air pressure under the body
curiosity-expansion-064.e: The bent pole works like a spring. Some of the energy from the run is stored briefly and released again as the pole straightens.

curiosity-expansion-065.p: Why do cyclists benefit from riding closely behind one another?
o: The riders at the back have less air resistance
Eddies push the back wheel forward
Tyre pressure rises for those behind
curiosity-expansion-065.e: The front rider pushes air to the sides and creates an area of lower resistance behind. That is why teams often take turns at the front.

curiosity-expansion-066.p: Why does a vacuum flask keep a drink hot for a long time?
o: A vacuum hinders conduction and air flow
A tight lid raises the boiling point
Glass turns heat radiation into light
curiosity-expansion-066.e: There is very little matter between the walls of the flask to conduct heat. Shiny surfaces also reduce heat transfer through radiation.

curiosity-expansion-067.p: What does the Y-shaped channel in a zip slider do?
o: It guides the teeth into each other
It presses the teeth flat and locks them
curiosity-expansion-067.e: The wedge-shaped channels of the slider guide the teeth or coils into a position where they interlock. Moving the slider the other way separates them again.

curiosity-expansion-068.p: Why does a pencil not contain ordinary lead in its core?
o: Graphite and clay make up the writing mass
The wood converts lead into carbon
The core is made of dried ink
curiosity-expansion-068.e: Graphite was historically confused with a form of lead. The mixture of graphite and clay determines, among other things, how hard and dark the line becomes.

curiosity-expansion-069.p: Why are many ancient statues missing their noses?
o: Noses were made of a different material
Museums removed them to date them
The middle of the face was ground away
curiosity-expansion-069.e: A nose protrudes and is therefore exposed to falls, transport and centuries of wear. Some statues were also deliberately damaged, but that does not explain every case.

curiosity-expansion-070.p: Which direction does an ordinary mirror actually reverse?
curiosity-expansion-070.e: The mirror reverses the depth direction: what points towards the mirror appears to point out. Left and right seem swapped because we imagine turning ourselves into the position of the reflection.

curiosity-expansion-071.p: Why can a CD show rainbow colours in the light?
o: Plastic layers each carry a pigment
curiosity-expansion-071.e: The microscopic, regular tracks act as an optical grating. Different wavelengths are reinforced in different directions.

curiosity-expansion-072.p: Why does a soap bubble show shifting rainbow colours?
o: Light from the thin film interferes
Soap splits water into coloured droplets
Air refracts the light like a prism
The bubble's curvature mirrors the sky
curiosity-expansion-072.e: Reflections from the outer and inner surfaces of the film meet. Depending on the film's thickness, some colours are reinforced while others are weakened.

curiosity-expansion-073.p: Why can canned food keep for a long time before the can is opened?
o: Heat and a sealed closure stop growth
curiosity-expansion-073.e: The heat treatment reduces harmful microorganisms, and the sealed container prevents new ones from getting in. A dented or swollen can should be discarded.

curiosity-expansion-074.p: What creates the illusion that a wheel in a film is turning backwards?
o: The spokes are captured at almost the same position
The shutter speed mirrors the movement
The lens delays the upper half
curiosity-expansion-074.e: A film shows a series of individual frames. If a spoke almost reaches the previous spoke's position between two frames, we perceive the shortest movement as backwards rotation.

curiosity-expansion-075.p: How can an audience spontaneously start clapping in the same rhythm?
o: Echoes move claps to the same beat
The audience's pulse sets the tempo
Loud claps hide beats out of time
curiosity-expansion-075.e: When people hear each other's claps, they make small timing adjustments. The mutual influence can gradually bring the group together around a shared pulse.

curiosity-round-3-002.p: Why are special-effects scenes often filmed in front of a green background?
o: Strong contrast to most skin tones
Less reflection in the camera lens
More even lighting of the actors
curiosity-round-3-002.e: A uniform colour can be selected digitally and replaced. Green is often used because sensors register it effectively and it rarely matches skin tones.

curiosity-round-3-004.p: Why does a guitar's tone change when the string is shortened with a finger?
o: A shorter vibrating length raises the pitch
Greater pressure makes the vibrations slower
The wood dampens the bright tones
curiosity-round-3-004.e: A shorter vibrating string has a higher fundamental frequency when the tension and thickness are otherwise roughly unchanged.

curiosity-round-3-005.p: Why can you feel a powerful bass note in your body?
o: Low frequencies move a lot of air
Deep tones travel through the floor
The ear sends bass on to the chest
curiosity-round-3-005.e: Large loudspeaker diaphragms can produce considerable pressure variations. At high volume, these are registered both by hearing and by the body's sense of touch.

curiosity-round-3-006.p: Why is a singer often recorded several times to the same chorus?
o: The software merges them into one perfect take
curiosity-round-3-006.e: Small differences in timing and pitch between takes create width. The technique is often called double tracking or vocal stacking.

curiosity-round-3-007.p: Why is very deep bass often cut from instruments other than the bass and kick drum?
o: More room in the mix's low end
Each instrument becomes clearer in solo
The instruments are moved out into stereo
curiosity-round-3-007.e: Many tracks contain unnecessary low-frequency rumble. A gentle high-pass filter can reduce build-up without changing the essential character of the instrument.

curiosity-round-3-008.p: Why can a short delay make a sound seem wider in stereo?
o: The time difference changes the perceived direction
curiosity-round-3-008.e: A small time difference between the left and right channels affects the perceived direction and can create width. Too large a difference is heard as a separate echo.

curiosity-round-3-009.p: Why can an online game feel delayed even when the picture runs smoothly?
o: The trip to the server takes time
The frame rate drops between inputs
The graphics card waits for the network
curiosity-round-3-009.e: Frame rate and network delay are different things. High latency means an action takes time to reach the server and return.

curiosity-round-3-010.p: Why does motion look smoother at a higher frame rate?
curiosity-round-3-010.e: More frames per second means less difference between each frame, and can also reduce the wait before new motion is shown.

curiosity-round-3-011.p: Why is the surface of a golf ball covered in small dimples?
o: They control the air layer around the ball
They give the ball more weight
They give better contact with the club
curiosity-round-3-011.e: The dimples control the air layer close to the ball, so the flow separates later. This reduces pressure drag and markedly improves the flight.

curiosity-round-3-012.p: Why is a tennis ball covered in felt?
o: It controls speed, spin and bounce
It keeps the pressure stable inside the ball
It makes contact with the racket longer
It protects the rubber from the sun's heat
curiosity-round-3-012.e: The felt slows the ball through the air and affects how spin grips. Without felt, the speed and trajectories of play would be very different.

curiosity-round-3-013.p: Why are the innermost lanes not always an advantage on a running track?
o: Staggered starts compensate for the distance
Outer lanes have a lower permitted speed
Inner lanes have a longer straight
The finish line slopes towards the outer side
curiosity-round-3-013.e: On races with bends, the outer lanes start further forward. The staggering compensates for their larger bend radius.

curiosity-round-3-014.p: Why can owls fly more silently than many other birds?
o: Fringes on the feathers dampen turbulence
The wing beats lie below hearing range
The underside directs the sound upwards
curiosity-round-3-014.e: Fine fringes and a soft surface on the wing feathers break up the airflow and reduce the noise that might otherwise warn prey.

curiosity-round-3-015.p: Why does a cat often lick its fur?
o: It adds fat from the tongue
curiosity-round-3-015.e: A cat's rough tongue removes loose hair and dirt. Saliva that evaporates from the fur can also help cool the animal.

curiosity-round-3-016.p: Why do ants often walk in clear trails behind one another?
o: Earth's magnetic field gives guide lines
curiosity-round-3-016.e: An ant can deposit pheromones on its way to food. When others follow and reinforce the trail, an efficient route for the whole colony emerges.

curiosity-round-3-017.p: Why does the arctic fox's coat change colour through the year?
o: White and brown give seasonal camouflage
Cold stops the production of pigment
Winter diet changes the hair colour
curiosity-round-3-017.e: The arctic fox moults between an often brownish summer coat and a white winter coat. The change is controlled partly by day length.

curiosity-round-3-018.p: Why do deciduous trees drop their leaves before winter?
o: To limit water loss when the ground is cold
To avoid leaves using oxygen at night
To send more sunlight down to the roots
To prevent green pigments from freezing
curiosity-round-3-018.e: Leaves lose a lot of water through evaporation. When the roots struggle to take up new water, the tree reuses nutrients and forms a layer that loosens the leaves.

curiosity-round-3-019.p: Why does snow often crunch most in hard frost?
o: Melt layers freeze with a snap
curiosity-round-3-019.e: At very low temperatures there is little liquid water between the crystals. They deform less and therefore break with distinct small sounds.

curiosity-round-3-020.p: Why does a river often wind more and more across a flat landscape?
o: Erosion on the outside, deposition on the inside
Wind presses the current against the bank
curiosity-round-3-020.e: Water flows faster along the outside of a bend and more slowly along the inside. The difference can gradually strengthen the river's meanders.

curiosity-round-3-021.p: Why are many large cities located by rivers or coasts?
o: Damp soil is easy to build on
curiosity-round-3-021.e: Before railways and lorries, ships were an efficient way to move heavy goods. Water also provided resources and connections to other areas.

curiosity-round-3-022.p: Why do wetlands help reduce flooding?
o: They store water and release it slowly
They channel water down to the groundwater
curiosity-round-3-022.e: Wetlands work as natural basins. They spread water over a larger area and delay some of the flow towards areas further downstream.

curiosity-round-3-023.p: Why can new forests not on their own stop climate change?
o: Area and carbon storage are limited
The forest releases the year's uptake in winter
Carbon remains locked even in a fire
curiosity-round-3-023.e: Forests store carbon, but there is limited space, and the store can be lost in forest fires or felling. Emissions must therefore also be reduced.

curiosity-round-3-025.p: Why does your voice often sound deeper when you have a cold?
curiosity-round-3-025.e: Irritated vocal folds can become thicker and vibrate more slowly. Blocked cavities also change how the voice resonates.

curiosity-round-3-026.p: Why does sleep often help learning?
o: New memories are processed and consolidated
The brain learns without the senses
curiosity-round-3-026.e: During sleep, patterns from the day's learning are reactivated, and connections in memory are organised. Sleep does not, however, replace the practice itself.

curiosity-round-3-027.p: Why does a task often feel easier after a break?
o: Focus is restored and thinking loosens
The problem moves to long-term storage
curiosity-round-3-027.e: A break can reduce mental fixation and fatigue. Sometimes unconscious processing continues, so a new approach becomes visible.

curiosity-round-3-028.p: Why do people often weigh a loss more heavily than an equal gain?
o: Gains are remembered for a shorter time
Money loses value when it is left
curiosity-round-3-028.e: The phenomenon is called loss aversion. It can influence choices, even when the gain and the loss are mathematically equal.

curiosity-round-3-030.p: Why does Denmark often have governments made up of several parties?
o: Seats are rarely held by a single party
The Danish Constitution requires several parties
Each region must have its own party
Parties may only field a few candidates
curiosity-round-3-030.e: Denmark's multi-party system makes an outright majority for a single party unusual. Parties therefore cooperate in coalitions or seek support as a minority government.

curiosity-round-3-032.p: Why did many medieval castles have narrow windows?
o: Small openings weakened the wall less
The glass of the time could not support itself
Darkness made the defenders hard to see
Smoke was kept inside in winter
curiosity-round-3-032.e: Thick walls and limited openings provided protection. Some narrow arrow slits allowed defenders to see and shoot out with less exposure.

curiosity-round-3-033.p: Why did the Romans build roads with a slightly arched surface?
o: Rainwater could run off to the sides
Soldiers could see the middle of the road better
curiosity-round-3-033.e: A raised road centre and ditches at the sides improved drainage. This protected the road's layers from becoming waterlogged and damaged.

curiosity-round-3-034.p: Why do distant mountains often look more bluish than the landscape close by?
o: Scattered light gives a bluish cast
The eye becomes less sensitive to red
curiosity-round-3-034.e: Air and small particles between us and the subject scatter light. The effect is called aerial perspective and is also used deliberately in paintings.

curiosity-round-3-035.p: Why does a drawing with a single vanishing point have clear depth?
o: Parallel lines meet in the distance
The paper curves around the point
Things get the same size diagonally
curiosity-round-3-035.e: Linear perspective imitates how the angle between parallel lines shrinks with distance. The brain interprets the pattern as spatial depth.

curiosity-round-3-037.p: Why does a barcode usually not contain the product's price?
o: The code points to the store's register
The price is calculated from the weight
Prices may not be printed on packaging
curiosity-round-3-037.e: A product code points to a record in the store's system. The price can therefore be changed centrally without printing a new code on every item.

curiosity-round-3-038.p: Why do companies often choose a very simple logo?
o: Lower tax on a few elements
Greater chance of an available trademark
curiosity-round-3-038.e: A simple shape can work on everything from a small app icon to a sign, and it is easier to recognise in a short time. However, it is not a fixed rule.

curiosity-round-3-039.p: Why does soup often become saltier as it boils down?
o: Steam presses salt down into the soup
curiosity-round-3-039.e: When the amount of liquid falls, roughly the same amount of salt is spread through less water. The concentration, and with it the saltiness, rises.

curiosity-round-3-040.p: Why does meat often rest for a few minutes after frying?
o: Resting time breaks down connective tissue
The meat soaks up liquid from the dish
curiosity-round-3-040.e: During resting the temperature briefly keeps moving inwards, and the pressure in the meat falls. Less juice therefore runs out at the first cut.

curiosity-round-3-041.p: Why should whipped cream ideally be whipped in a cold bowl?
o: A cold bowl adds more oxygen
curiosity-round-3-041.e: Whipping works air into the cream, which is held in place by a network of fat globules. If the temperature is too high, the fat becomes too soft to stabilise the foam effectively.

curiosity-round-3-042.p: Why can you smell a wine more when the glass is gently swirled?
o: A larger surface gives more aroma
The movement creates new aroma compounds
Rotation pushes out the carbon dioxide
The glass filters out sharp smells
curiosity-round-3-042.e: When the wine spreads as a thin film on the inside of the glass, more aroma molecules evaporate and gather in the air above the wine.

curiosity-round-3-043.p: Why should you keep a greater distance to the car ahead on a wet road?
o: Less grip lengthens the braking distance
Rain reduces the mechanical pressure of the brakes
curiosity-round-3-043.e: Water reduces friction between tyres and road, and with a lot of water the tyre can lose contact completely. Reaction time is the same, but stopping takes longer.

curiosity-round-3-044.p: Why are aircraft wings curved and slightly angled into the airflow?
o: The wing deflects air and lifts the plane
The curve gathers slow air like a cushion
The angle moves the centre of gravity down
The upper side pushes the pressure away
curiosity-round-3-044.e: The wing's shape and angle change the speed and direction of the air around it. Pressure differences and a downward flow of air together create lift.

curiosity-round-3-045.p: Why is the triangle widely used in bridges and lattice structures?
o: It cannot be pushed out of shape
Diagonal bars spread the weight evenly
The triangle carries the load straight down
Three joints use the least material
curiosity-round-3-045.e: A rectangular frame can skew out of shape, while a triangle is geometrically stable. Forces can be carried as tension and compression through the bars.

curiosity-round-3-046.p: Why do concert halls often have uneven walls and ceilings?
o: Sloping surfaces direct sound towards the stage
curiosity-round-3-046.e: Diffusion reduces sharp echoes and helps sound reach the audience more evenly. The shape is designed together with absorbent materials.

curiosity-round-3-047.p: What does the thought experiment about a ship whose parts are all replaced investigate?
o: Whether a thing remains the same
Whether ownership follows the oldest part
Whether a copy inherits the history
curiosity-round-3-047.e: The Ship of Theseus challenges the idea of identity: is something still the same when all its parts have gradually been replaced?

curiosity-round-3-050.p: Why is a football pitch sometimes watered shortly before a match?
o: Less friction gives a faster roll
Moisture makes the pitch lines more precise
curiosity-round-3-050.e: Light watering can reduce friction between the ball and the grass and give a faster passing game. Too much water naturally has the opposite effect.

curiosity-round-3-051.p: Why does the light-reflecting layer in a reindeer's eye change colour in winter?
o: Sight becomes more sensitive to light
It protects against the heat of the northern lights
It hides the gaze from predators
curiosity-round-3-051.e: The reindeer's tapetum lucidum changes from golden in summer to deep blue in winter. The change helps the eye make use of very faint light.

curiosity-round-3-052.p: According to Greek mythology, why did Atlas have to carry the heavens?
o: He lost a fight against Heracles
He refused to join the Argonauts
curiosity-round-3-052.e: After the defeat of the Titans in the Titanomachy, Zeus condemned Atlas to carry the sky. In the earliest sources he does not carry the Earth itself.

curiosity-round-3-053.p: Why could the nymph Echo, according to the myth, only repeat other people's last words?
o: Pan made her into a voice
curiosity-round-3-053.e: In Ovid's version, Echo kept Hera busy with chatter. As punishment she could then only repeat the endings of other people's speech.

curiosity-round-3-054.p: Why did Thor's hammer have an unusually short handle in the myth?
o: Thor broke the handle in battle
Odin wanted it kept in one hand
Giants stole the metal from the handle
curiosity-round-3-054.e: In the Skáldskaparmál, Loki disguised himself as a fly and stung the smith Brokkr. The interruption became the reason for Mjölnir's short handle.

curiosity-round-3-055.p: Why did Harry survive Voldemort's attack as a baby?
o: His mother's voluntary sacrifice gave protection
The wand would not attack a child
curiosity-round-3-055.e: Lily Potter's voluntary sacrifice left a protection that made Voldemort's killing curse rebound.

curiosity-round-3-057.p: Which natural event does Carl Nielsen's Helios Overture depict?
o: The sun rising and setting over the Aegean Sea
A storm over the west coast of Jutland
curiosity-round-3-057.e: Carl Nielsen wrote the work during a stay in Athens. The music follows the sun from the moment it breaks through over the sea until it sinks again.

curiosity-round-3-058.p: What is the veil of ignorance meant to help us do in John Rawls' thought experiment?
o: Choose rules without knowing our place
